title: The Milkmaid and the Pot of Milk
text:
Perrette set off for the town market with a pot of milk balanced on her head, on a cushion. She had dressed lightly and worn flat shoes so she could walk fast, and as she walked, she counted up her future.

With the money for the milk, she would buy a hundred eggs. The eggs would hatch into chicks; with care, she could raise three broods. The fox would have to be clever indeed to leave her too few to buy a pig. A pig costs little to fatten, and she would sell it for good money. With that she would buy a cow and a calf, and she could already see the calf frisking among the flock.

At that thought Perrette gave a little jump of joy. The pot fell from her head, and the milk ran out onto the road. Goodbye calf, cow, pig and chicks. She went home to explain herself to her husband, at the risk of a beating.

La Fontaine adds that everyone builds castles in the air like this, the wise as well as the foolish. He admits that he does it himself, and is a great king in his dreams, until some accident brings him back to what he really is.
lesson: Plan for the future, but keep your eyes on the step in front of you. Celebrating gains you have not secured is the surest way to lose them.
source: Jean de La Fontaine, Fables, Book VII (La Laitiere et le pot au lait); older versions in the Panchatantra
caveat: Fable numbering within Book VII differs between editions.
